sections.text: Self-employment tax is the Social Security and Medicare tax you pay on your own business profit. The IRS sets it at 12.4% for Social Security plus 2.9% for Medicare, a combined 15.3%, and it applies to 92.35% of your net earnings. In practice that works out to about 14.13% of your net profit until the Social Security cap applies. It is separate from income tax, and you pay both. This guide shows the arithmetic, what actually lowers the bill, and where a simple calculation stops being accurate.

Tax limits change every year. This guide states only the rates and rules published on the IRS self-employment tax page (12.4%, 2.9%, 92.35%, the $400 filing trigger and the half-tax deduction). It does not state the current Social Security wage base, additional Medicare thresholds, or estimated-payment dates, because they change. Check irs.gov for the current year before you file.
Where the 15.3% and the 92.35% come from

An employee pays half of the payroll tax and the employer pays the other half. That is 7.65% each: 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare. When you work for yourself you are both, so you pay 12.4% plus 2.9%. The IRS says that you usually must pay self-employment tax if your net earnings from self-employment were $400 or more.

The 92.35% figure puts you on equal footing with an employee, whose employer-paid half is not counted as wages. It equals 100% minus 7.65% (1 - 0.0765 = 0.9235). So the formula is: net profit x 0.9235 x 0.153. The IRS also lets you deduct one-half of the self-employment tax when you work out your adjusted gross income on Form 1040. That deduction lowers your income tax, not the self-employment tax itself.

The table applies the formula to four net profits. It assumes each profit is below the Social Security wage base for the year, so the full 12.4% applies. It also assumes no wages from a job. Results are rounded to the cent, as the Self-Employment Tax Calculator does.

The effective rate is 14.13% at every level in this range, because the formula is a flat percentage. Compare that with an employee earning $100,000 in wages: the employee sees $7,650 withheld, while the employer separately pays another $7,650. The self-employed person at $100,000 profit pays $14,129.55 in one bill. The total payroll tax load is similar. What changes is that you see the whole cost.
What the cap does to the calculation

The Social Security part stops at an annual wage base set by law, while the Medicare part has no cap. The IRS page says this amount changes annually, so use the current figure from irs.gov. To show the mechanism, here is a hypothetical: assume a cap of $150,000 (an invented number for illustration only) and a net profit of $200,000.

sections.text: Above the cap, each extra dollar of profit adds only the 2.9% Medicare portion (applied to 92.35% of the profit), which is why the effective rate falls. If you also earn wages, those wages count toward the Social Security base first, so your self-employment income may hit the cap sooner.
What lowers the bill, and what only moves it

items: Legitimate business expenses reduce net profit, and so reduce self-employment tax. Each $1,000 of deductible expense at the $100,000 level lowers SE tax by about $141.30 (0.9235 x 0.153 x $1,000), plus whatever income tax it saves.

The deductible half is not a credit. At an assumed 22% income tax rate (an assumption, not your rate), deducting $7,064.78 saves about $1,554.25, so the real net cost of the $14,129.55 is roughly $12,575, or 12.6% of profit.
A deduction for qualified business income may reduce your income tax. It does not reduce self-employment tax. Eligibility and limits depend on your situation, so check the IRS rules.

Retirement contributions for the self-employed generally reduce income tax. Whether they also reduce SE tax depends on the plan type, so confirm with the IRS or a tax professional before assuming either way.

sections.text: Common mistakes and when the simple formula fails

items: Setting aside only the SE tax. It is one of two bills. Income tax comes on top, and many states and countries add their own.
Using revenue instead of net profit. The formula applies to profit after expenses, not to what clients paid you.

Forgetting you may owe estimated payments during the year. The IRS expects tax to be paid as you earn, usually in quarterly installments, and underpaying can trigger a penalty. Get the current due dates from the IRS.
Ignoring the additional Medicare tax on high earnings and any wages you also have. The simple calculator does not model them.
Assuming this applies outside the United States. Self-employment contributions in other countries use different rules and rates.

sections.text: This is a general explanation using the published IRS formula, not tax advice. Partnerships, farm income, church employee income, and business structures such as S corporations can change the calculation. If your situation is anything other than a single sole proprietorship, talk to a qualified tax professional.
